concept: Neurodegeneration mechanisms: proteostasis, mitochondria and neuroinflammation

claims.text: The Mouton-Liger review describes proteasomal and lysosomal pathways that degrade damaged mitochondrial components outside mitochondria. (low confidence)

In dopaminergic neurons derived from patients with idiopathic and familial Parkinson’s disease, Burbulla and colleagues report a cascade linking mitochondrial oxidant stress through oxidized dopamine accumulation to reduced glucocerebrosidase activity and lysosomal dysfunction. (low confidence)
Burbulla and colleagues report that the toxic cascade was observed in human but not mouse Parkinson’s disease neurons, partly because of species-specific dopamine metabolism. (low confidence)

Wang and Xu propose that upstream PINK1/Parkin activation can become partly uncoupled from downstream mitochondrial clearance under Parkinson’s disease-relevant conditions; pathway activation therefore does not necessarily demonstrate completed mitophagy. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-24)
The Mouton-Liger review describes excessive microglial activation in postmortem Parkinson’s disease brains as a feature of brain neuroinflammation. (low confidence)

Brochard and colleagues report brain infiltration by CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, but not B cells, in postmortem human Parkinson disease specimens and in the MPTP mouse model during neuronal degeneration. (low confidence)
Sulzer and colleagues report that α-synuclein-derived peptides act as antigenic epitopes driving helper and cytotoxic T cell responses in patients with Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence)
Within the MPTP mouse model, Brochard and colleagues attribute T cell-mediated dopaminergic toxicity predominantly to CD4+ T cells requiring FasL expression rather than IFNγ. (low confidence)

Mazzulli and colleagues report that functional loss of glucocerebrosidase compromises lysosomal protein degradation in primary cultures or human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons. (low confidence)

The Mouton-Liger review describes mammalian-cell evidence that PINK1 and Parkin jointly regulate clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria through autophagy and lysosomal degradation, termed mitophagy. (low confidence)

McWilliams and colleagues report that loss of Pink1 did not alter basal mitophagy in the mouse tissues examined apart from pancreatic islets; this limits extrapolation from depolarization-induced pathway activation to basal mitochondrial turnover. (low confidence)
Brochard and colleagues report attenuation of MPTP-induced dopaminergic cell death in mice lacking CD4. (low confidence)

narrative.documentConcept: Neurodegeneration mechanisms: proteostasis, mitochondria and neuroinflammation
narrative.text: Research connects impaired protein degradation, mitochondrial quality control and inflammatory responses in Parkinson’s disease. Patient-derived neuronal studies link dopamine oxidation to mitochondrial and lysosomal dysfunction. Mouse experiments distinguish basal mitochondrial turnover from stress-induced mitophagy and probe immune contributions to neuronal death. Human immune observations and model findings have different causal scope; pathway activation alone does not establish completed mitochondrial clearance.
